rounds.proof_sketch: total_output_elements = 16 × 32 × output_d × output_h × output_w. Since 16×32=512 is divisible by 256, and output dimensions are integers, total_output_elements is always divisible by elements_per_block=256. Therefore linear_idx never equals total_output_elements inside the loop—the loop condition linear_idx < start_idx+256 prevents it. The >= vs > check is never triggered.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary guard from >= to >, which would only cause different behavior when linear_idx exactly equals total_output_elements. However, due to the fixed input shape [16, 32, 64, 64, 64] having batch_size=16 and channels=32, the product 16×32=512 is divisible by 256 (elements_per_block). This means total_output_elements is always a multiple of 256 regardless of pooling parameters. When total_output_elements is divisible by elements_per_block, the last block processes exactly the remaining valid elements, and no thread ever reaches linear_idx=total_output_elements within the loop bounds. The boundary check becomes dead code that never triggers.
rounds.kill_strategy: Requires changing batch_size or channels to make total_output_elements not divisible by 256, which violates the fixed-shape contract. No value-level test can kill this mutant.
rounds.recommendations: When designing mutation tests for GPU kernels with block-level parallelism, include test shapes where total_elements % elements_per_block ≠ 0 to exercise boundary guard code paths. Consider using prime-number batch sizes (e.g., 17) or channels (e.g., 31) to ensure boundary conditions are reachable.
